title: Automated KV/prefix caching heuristics and safe rollout for cost-driven inference
creator: Claire Nguyen
description: Goal: build an automated recommendation and safe-apply system for KV/prefix caching that optimizes per-token cost while preserving latency SLOs and output quality. This ticket scopes the heuristics, simulation model, rollout plan, and the fail-safe rollback triggers for applying TTL and keying changes across workloads. Background: manual TTL and key design tuning has driven inconsistent wins — large variance in hit rate across customers and routes, and operational risk during broad config pushes. We will deliver a conservative, data-driven autotuner that: recommends key shapes, TTLs, and cache policies per-route; simulates expected cost/latency tradeoffs; provides a safe canary/circuit-breaker apply flow with automated rollback based on telemetry; and exposes simple tuning knobs in Console + API for ops and SREs.
acceptance_criteria: A simulator that ingests historical request traces and outputs per-route: projected hit rate, expected token savings, and 95th percentile added latency distribution
Automated suggestion engine that produces a recommended config (key template + TTL + policy) and a confidence score for each route
Safe-apply pipeline implemented: canary rollout on 1% of traffic, automated health checks and rollback triggers (error rate, 95p latency spike, token-cost increase), and manual override
Integrations: Console UI panel showing recommendations; API to apply recommendations; metrics in Grafana and an evaluation dashboard for experiments
Documented playbook for engineers/SEs outlining rollout steps, rollback thresholds, and post-rollout validation queries
tasks: Instrument request traces to include prefix-hash, sequence-length, and model-variant metadata if missing
Implement hit-rate simulator that can replay traces with configurable TTL and keying rules
Design recommendation heuristics: baseline heuristics include frequency-based TTL, decayed per-prefix score, and cost-aware TTL via marginal-token-saved per-second
Build safe-apply control-plane: feature flag, rollout orchestration, canary policy, and automated rollback hooks
Add observability: per-route cost delta, hit-rate, cache-size, 95p latency, and anomaly detectors tied to rollouts
Ship Console UI: recommendations list, one-click apply to canary, and rollback button
notes: Key design principle: prefer conservative changes that reduce cost while limiting potential QoS regressions. Start with per-route TTL decreases rather than global increases to cache scope.
We should model the marginal benefit of extending TTL by 100ms/1s/10s buckets instead of only absolute TTL values to capture diminishing returns for long-lived prefixes.

For key shaping: recommend separating 'user-bounded' vs 'session-bounded' prefixes; avoid including ephemeral vectors (e.g., ephemeral_request_id) in keys; canonicalize prompt prefixes by normalizing user metadata fields.
Avoid automated cross-model key reuse until model compatibility matrix is validated (different quantization/kernels can change KV semantics).
Consider a fallback to 'miss-only batching' when a canary increases upstream latency: temporarily batch only the misses to flatten cost spike while rollback proceeds.
simulation_approach: Input: past 7-30 days of request traces per-route (timestamp, prefix-hash, token-count, model, response-latency, outcome) as ndjson
For each candidate config, replay chronologically and maintain an LRU/ttl map to compute hit/miss and aggregated token savings and added per-request latency (due to cache-check overhead)
Model cold-start warmup by seeding top-N prefixes based on recency-weighted frequency to estimate warm caches during canary
Output: hit_rate_time_series, token_saved_total, ops_on_backend, expected added latency distribution, and suggested rollback probabilistic impact
heuristics_summary: Frequency-first TTL: assign base TTL proportional to prefix frequency with caps per-model and per-route
Cost-aware TTL: compute expected tokens_saved_per_sec = prefix_freq * avg_tokens * probability_of_repeat; map to TTL bands that meet target ROI threshold
Prefix-merging: auto-suggest merging low-frequency sibling prefixes into a coarser key shape when combined hit rate shows net positive cost outcome
Safety multipliers: reduce suggested TTL by 0.7x for routes with strict 95p latency SLOs or known flakey models
Decay windows: prefer time-decay weighting to focus autotuner on recent behavior during high-growth or seasonality
rollout_plan: Stage 1 - Offline simulation and recommendation vetting (this ticket)
Stage 2 - Internal canary: apply to internal traffic/domains for 48-72 hours with full telemetry
Stage 3 - Customer canary: 1% traffic for selected customers, monitor for 24-72 hours
Stage 4 - Ramp: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated gates at each step and manual approval for major changes
Rollback triggers: >=10% relative increase in 95p latency, >=3% absolute error-rate increase, unexpected token cost increase > 5% over 1h
observability_and_alerting: Dashboards: per-route cache hit/miss, token savings, backend RPS, and latency percentiles
Alert rules: guard rails tied to rollout (e.g., rapid 95p latency spike during canary triggers immediate rollback), and anomaly detection on hit-rate divergence
Postmortem metrics to capture: time-to-rollout, time-to-rollback, customer-reported quality regressions, and realized cost savings after 7/30 days
ui_and_api_contracts: POST /v1/kv-recommendations - accepts route_id and time-window, returns list of candidate configs with confidence scores
POST /v1/kv-rollouts - start rollout specifying percent and auto-rollback thresholds
Console panel: Recommendation card shows expected annualized token savings, hit-rate uplift delta, and risk indicators (latency risk, model-compatibility risk)
Audit log entry schema for applies and rollbacks to satisfy compliance requests
open_questions: How to represent multi-tenant shared caches vs per-tenant caches in the recommendation engine? Should we bias TTLs to protect noisy neighbors?
What is the canonical cost model to attribute savings for multi-variant responses that share prefixes? (e.g., reranking followed by expansion)
Should we allow recommendations that change key shape (coarsening) automatically, or require explicit human approval for key-shape changes?
Do we want a default safe TTL floor (e.g., 100ms) to avoid extremely aggressive evictions that increase backend load?
